Figure 3 — Validation MAE (US$) of every configuration, mean ± standard deviation over 5 seeds, sorted from best (top) to worst. Colors mark where each configuration comes from. Dashed line: Ridge on validation (57.85); dotted line: 5% below Ridge (54.96), the margin the Stage 0 criterion asks for on the test set.

Reading Figure 3 and the table.

  • What wins is capacity with regularization. The top 3 all have 3 hidden layers and dropout of 0.2 or more. Without regularization, more width hurts: 256 → 128 alone is last (56.13), and the same network with dropout 0.2 is eighth (55.38).
  • The learning rate of Stage 3 holds. Around 256 → 128 with dropout 0.2, both 3e-3 (55.53) and 3e-4 (55.54) are worse than 1e-3 (55.38).
  • Round 2 found a plateau, which is why the search stops there. Going from dropout 0.3 to 0.4 changes nothing (55.09 and 55.09). Doubling the width (55.23) or adding a fourth layer (55.32) does not help and makes the result less stable (std 0.32 and 0.40).
  • The choice is a tie. By the rule, dropout 0.4 is first (55.086 against 55.095, see search_numbers.json), but the gap is about 0.01 for a standard deviation of 0.15. The two are equivalent and the rule decides.
  • Gain over the base network: US$ 0.75 (55.84 → 55.09). The chosen network has 211,457 parameters for 31,285 training rows — more parameters than rows; dropout 0.4 and early stopping are what keep it from memorizing the training set.
  • Already on validation, the margin is short of 5%: the chosen network is 4.77% below Ridge (57.85 → 55.09), to the left of the dashed line but not of the dotted one. Before opening the test set, the expectation was therefore a borderline result.

Chosen configuration, saved in code/best_config.json with only the keys that change with respect to BASE_CONFIG:

{"hidden": [512, 256, 128], "dropout": 0.4}

That is, 3 hidden layers of 512 → 256 → 128 units (ReLU, He initialization), dropout 0.4 after each hidden layer, no weight decay, no BatchNorm; AdamW with learning rate 1e-3, batch 256, Huber loss, early stopping with patience 15.

docs.title: 5 · Test evaluation
docs.text:
Script: code/evaluate.py.

How the test set was used — once.

  1. Everything was fixed before the test set was loaded: the configuration (best_config.json, Stage 4), the seeds (42 to 46), the metrics, the figures and the decision rule for the criterion (mean test MAE over the 5 seeds against the best baseline's test MAE).
  2. The script was developed on validation: without arguments, evaluate.py runs the whole evaluation on the validation set and writes nothing. That run reproduced Stage 4 exactly (55.09 ± 0.15), which confirms that retraining is deterministic. The figure and CSV code was also checked on validation predictions.
  3. Then the script ran once with --split test — the only time Stages 0 to 5 loaded the test set (load_data(with_test=True)). Nothing was changed after it — no configuration, seed, threshold or figure choice was influenced by the test set. Running the command again reproduces the same numbers; it is not a new decision.

Protocol. For each seed, the chosen network is trained from scratch on the 31,285 training rows, with early stopping on validation — the same protocol under which it was selected. It is not retrained on train + validation, because early stopping needs the validation set and the number of epochs would otherwise have to be guessed. Dummy and Ridge are refitted on the same training rows with their Stage 1 settings. All models are evaluated on the same 9,777 test listings.

code/evaluate.py 
"""Stage 5: the chosen configuration, retrained with 5 seeds, evaluated ONCE on the test set.

Run from the repository root:

    python docs/projects/regression/code/evaluate.py               # development: validation
    python docs/projects/regression/code/evaluate.py --split test  # the single test run

The default run uses validation only and writes nothing; it exists so the script can be
developed and debugged without touching the test set. `--split test` reads
best_config.json (decided in Stage 4), produces Figures 4 and 5, test_numbers.json and
test_predictions.csv (read by Stage 6).
"""

import argparse
import json

import matplotlib

matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt  # noqa: E402
import numpy as np  # noqa: E402
import pandas as pd  # noqa: E402

from baselines import fit_baselines  # noqa: E402
from data import CODE_DIR, FIG_DIR, load_data, regression_metrics, to_log, to_price  # noqa: E402
from model import count_parameters  # noqa: E402
from search import BEST_JSON, SEEDS, TARGET_GAIN, label, summarize  # noqa: E402
from train import BASE_CONFIG, predict_price, train_model  # noqa: E402

OUT_JSON = CODE_DIR / "test_numbers.json"
OUT_CSV = CODE_DIR / "test_predictions.csv"
CSV_SEED = 42
N_RESIDUAL_BINS = 5  # quintiles of the predicted price, for reading Figure 5


def eval_split(d, split):
    if split == "test":
        return d["X_test"], d["y_test"], d["raw_test"]
    return d["X_val"], d["y_val"], d["raw_val"]


def train_seeds(d, config, X_eval, y_eval):
    """Retrain the chosen configuration once per seed; early stopping on validation."""
    y_tr, y_va = to_log(d["y_train"]), to_log(d["y_val"])
    runs, preds, n_params = [], {}, None
    for seed in SEEDS:
        model, h = train_model(d["X_train"], y_tr, d["X_val"], y_va, config, seed)
        preds[seed] = predict_price(model, X_eval)
        n_params = count_parameters(model)
        runs.append({"seed": seed, **regression_metrics(y_eval, preds[seed]),
                     "best_epoch": h["best_epoch"], "stopped_epoch": h["stopped_epoch"]})
    return runs, preds, n_params


def criterion(mean, std, runs, baselines):
    """Stage 0 criterion and the gap to the best baseline against the seed variation."""
    best_name = min(baselines, key=lambda k: baselines[k]["mae"])
    base_mae = baselines[best_name]["mae"]
    gap = base_mae - mean["mae"]
    return {
        "best_baseline": best_name,
        "best_baseline_mae": base_mae,
        "threshold_mae": (1 - TARGET_GAIN) * base_mae,
        "gain_mean": 1 - mean["mae"] / base_mae,
        "gain_per_seed": {str(r["seed"]): 1 - r["mae"] / base_mae for r in runs},
        "seeds_meeting_criterion": sum(r["mae"] <= (1 - TARGET_GAIN) * base_mae for r in runs),
        "met": bool(mean["mae"] <= (1 - TARGET_GAIN) * base_mae),
        "gap_mae": gap,
        "gap_over_seed_std": gap / std["mae"],
        "worst_seed_mae": max(r["mae"] for r in runs),
        "all_seeds_beat_baseline": all(r["mae"] < base_mae for r in runs),
    }


def residual_summary(y_true, y_pred):
    """Bias of the predictions, overall and per quintile of the predicted price."""
    res = y_true - y_pred
    bins = pd.qcut(y_pred, q=N_RESIDUAL_BINS)
    per_bin = pd.DataFrame({"res": res, "bin": bins}).groupby("bin", observed=True)["res"]
    return {
        "mean_residual": float(res.mean()),
        "median_residual": float(np.median(res)),
        "share_underpredicted": float((res > 0).mean()),
        "mean_log_residual": float(np.mean(np.log1p(y_true) - np.log1p(y_pred))),
        "by_predicted_quintile": [
            {"pred_from": float(b.left), "pred_to": float(b.right),
             "median_residual": float(g.median()), "mean_residual": float(g.mean())}
            for b, g in per_bin
        ],
    }


def plot_pred_vs_actual(y_true, preds, name):
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4.6), sharex=True, sharey=True)
    lims = (8, 12000)
    for ax, (title, y_pred) in zip(axes, preds.items()):
        ax.scatter(y_true, y_pred, s=4, alpha=0.15, label="test listings")
        ax.plot(lims, lims, color="black", ls="--", label="perfect prediction (y = x)")
        ax.set(title=title, xscale="log", yscale="log", xlim=lims, ylim=lims,
               xlabel="actual price (US$, log scale)")
        ax.legend(loc="upper left", fontsize=8)
    axes[0].set_ylabel("predicted price (US$, log scale)")
    fig.suptitle("Predicted × actual price on the test set")
    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig(FIG_DIR / name, dpi=110)
    plt.close(fig)


def plot_residuals(y_true, y_pred, name):
    res = y_true - y_pred
    bins = pd.qcut(y_pred, q=N_RESIDUAL_BINS)
    grouped = pd.DataFrame({"p": y_pred, "r": res, "b": bins}).groupby("b", observed=True)
    med, avg = grouped.median(), grouped.mean()
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.6))
    ax.scatter(y_pred, res, s=4, alpha=0.15, label="test listings")
    ax.axhline(0, color="black", ls="--", label="zero residual")
    ax.plot(med["p"], med["r"], color="red", marker="o",
            label="median residual per predicted-price quintile")
    ax.plot(med["p"], avg["r"], color="darkorange", marker="s",
            label="mean residual per predicted-price quintile")
    ax.set(title="Residual (actual − predicted) × predicted price, test set, network seed 42",
           xscale="log", xlabel="predicted price (US$, log scale)",
           ylabel="residual (US$, symlog: linear in ±100)")
    ax.set_yscale("symlog", linthresh=100)
    ax.legend(loc="lower left", fontsize=8)
    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig(FIG_DIR / name, dpi=110)
    plt.close(fig)


def write_predictions(raw_eval, y_eval, net_pred, base_preds):
    pd.DataFrame({
        "row_index": raw_eval.index,  # row of data/AB_NYC_2019.csv (0-based)
        "price_true": y_eval,
        "price_pred": net_pred,
        "pred_ridge": base_preds["ridge"],
        "pred_dummy": base_preds["dummy_mean"],
    }).to_csv(OUT_CSV, index=False)


def main():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__.splitlines()[0])
    parser.add_argument("--split", choices=["val", "test"], default="val")
    split = parser.parse_args().split

    best = json.loads(BEST_JSON.read_text())
    config = {**BASE_CONFIG, **best}
    d = load_data(with_test=(split == "test"))
    X_eval, y_eval, raw_eval = eval_split(d, split)

    models = fit_baselines(d["X_train"], d["y_train"])
    base_preds = {name: to_price(m.predict(X_eval)) for name, m in models.items()}
    baselines = {name: regression_metrics(y_eval, p) for name, p in base_preds.items()}
    runs, preds, n_params = train_seeds(d, best, X_eval, y_eval)
    mean, std = summarize(runs)

    numbers = {
        "split": split,
        "config": config,
        "label": label(best),
        "parameters": n_params,
        "seeds": list(SEEDS),
        "rows": len(y_eval),
        "baselines": baselines,
        "network": {"mean": mean, "std": std, "runs": runs},
        "criterion": criterion(mean, std, runs, baselines),
        "residuals_seed_42": residual_summary(y_eval, preds[CSV_SEED]),
    }
    print(json.dumps({k: numbers[k] for k in ("baselines", "criterion")}, indent=2))
    print("network mean:", json.dumps(mean), "\nnetwork std:", json.dumps(std))
    if split != "test":
        print("validation run: nothing written. Use --split test for the single test run.")
        return

    OUT_JSON.write_text(json.dumps(numbers, indent=2))
    write_predictions(raw_eval, y_eval, preds[CSV_SEED], base_preds)
    plot_pred_vs_actual(y_eval, {"MLP (seed 42)": preds[CSV_SEED],
                                 "Ridge (best baseline)": base_preds["ridge"]},
                        "fig04-pred-vs-actual.png")
    plot_residuals(y_eval, preds[CSV_SEED], "fig05-residuals.png")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
Model (test set, 9,777 rows) MAE (US$) RMSE (US$) R² (US$) RMSE in log Dummy (mean) 82.12 222.21 −0.029 0.685 Ridge (best baseline) 58.13 203.52 0.137 0.453 MLP 512-256-128, dropout 0.4 (5 seeds) 55.28 ± 0.08 202.18 ± 0.62 0.148 ± 0.005 0.436 ± 0.001 Seed Test MAE (US$) Below Ridge Best epoch Stopped at 42 55.23 4.99% 69 84 43 55.38 4.74% 73 88 44 55.36 4.77% 74 89 45 55.26 4.94% 59 74 46 55.19 5.06% 48 63

Was the Stage 0 criterion met? No. The criterion asks for a test MAE at least 5% below the best baseline: 0.95 × 58.13 = US$ 55.22. The network's mean test MAE is 55.28, 4.90% below Ridge — US$ 0.06 short of the threshold. Only one seed of the five (46, 5.06%) passes on its own; picking it would mean choosing a seed by looking at the test set, so the decision stays on the mean, as fixed in advance. The criterion is not changed.

Is the gap to Ridge larger than the variation between seeds? Yes, by far. The network is US$ 2.85 better than Ridge in mean MAE, and the standard deviation across seeds is US$ 0.08 — the gap is 34.6 times the seed variation, and every one of the 5 seeds beats Ridge (the worst seed has 55.38 against 58.13). So the improvement is real with respect to training randomness; it is only smaller than the 5% we had asked for. The seed standard deviation measures only training randomness, not which listings happened to fall in the test set.

Validation and test agree. On validation the chosen network was 4.77% below Ridge; on test it is 4.90%. Selecting 1 configuration out of 19 on validation did not produce an optimistic validation number that collapsed on test.

RMSE and R² tell a smaller story than MAE. In RMSE the network gains little over Ridge (202.18 against 203.52) and R² in US$ stays low (0.148 against 0.137). Both are dominated by the luxury tail, as anticipated in Stage 0: the gain of the network is in the typical listing, which is what MAE measures. In log scale the gain is clearer (RMSE 0.436 against 0.453).

Output for Stage 6. code/test_predictions.csv has one row per test listing: row_index (row of data/AB_NYC_2019.csv, 0-based, to join with the raw features), price_true, price_pred (network, seed 42), pred_ridge and pred_dummy, all in US$. code/test_numbers.json holds every number of this section.

Figure 4 — Predicted × actual price on the test set (both axes in log scale), for the network (seed 42, left) and for Ridge (right). Each point is a listing; the dashed line is a perfect prediction.

Reading Figure 4.

  • Both clouds are flatter than the diagonal: cheap listings are overpredicted and expensive ones underpredicted. That is what a model does when the features explain only part of the price — it pulls predictions towards the middle.
  • Listings priced between US$ 1,000 and US$ 10,000 are predicted at a few hundred dollars by both models. The EDA had already found that no feature identifies them, so neither model can.
  • The network's cloud reaches higher predictions than Ridge's (its highest test prediction is US$ 984.94): it can combine location and room type nonlinearly, while Ridge only adds their effects in log scale.

Figure 5 — Residual (actual − predicted price, US$) × predicted price, test set, network with seed 42. The y axis is linear between −100 and +100 and logarithmic beyond; the x axis is logarithmic. Red: median residual per quintile of the predicted price; orange: mean residual per quintile.

Reading Figure 5.

  • The network is unbiased for the typical listing. The median residual per predicted quintile stays between −2.98 and +3.59 US\(**, and the overall median residual is **−1.00 US\), with 48.9% of the listings underpredicted. That is the expected behaviour of a model trained on log1p(price): back on the US$ scale, its prediction behaves like a conditional median, which is what minimizes MAE.
  • The mean tells a different story: the mean residual is **+26.39 US\(**, and per quintile it grows from **+4.43** (cheapest predictions, up to US\) 66.16) to +60.82 (most expensive, above US$ 174.71). A few listings far above their prediction pull the mean up — the same luxury tail that keeps RMSE and R² low.
  • The error grows with the predicted price (the cloud opens to the right): the model is less certain in absolute dollars where prices are higher.
  • The diagonal stripes are listings with round prices (US$ 100, 150, 200...): for a fixed actual price, the residual falls linearly as the prediction rises.

docs.title: 6 · Error analysis
docs.text:
This section reads the test predictions Stage 5 wrote (code/test_predictions.csv, seed 42): MAE US$ 55.23 against Ridge's US$ 58.13 on the same 9,777 rows. No new prediction is made on the test set here.

The permutation importance is the one exception: shuffling ten columns five times each is a repeated probe, not a single evaluation, so it runs on the validation set, with the chosen configuration retrained at seed 42 (validation MAE US$ 55.20).

Every subgroup is also measured against Ridge on the same rows — "the network errs more here" only means something next to what the best baseline does with the same listings. Bias is the mean of (prediction − true price): negative means the network asks for less than the listing charges.

code/error_analysis.py 
"""Stage 6: error analysis — subgroups, worst cases and permutation importance.

Run from the repository root:  python docs/projects/regression/code/error_analysis.py

Two modes, chosen automatically from the files Stage 5 leaves in `code/`:

* **final** — `best_config.json` and `test_predictions.csv` both exist. The subgroup and
  worst-case analysis reads the **test** predictions written by Stage 5, so no new
  prediction is made on the test set here, and the permutation importance uses the chosen
  configuration retrained with seed 42.
* **provisional** — either file is missing. Everything runs on the **validation** set with
  the base network of Stage 3, so that the script can be written and checked before
  Stage 5 lands. Numbers from this mode do not go into the report.

The permutation importance always runs on the **validation** set, in both modes: the test
set is evaluated once, in Stage 5, and shuffling ten columns five times each is a repeated
probe, not a single evaluation.

Subgroups follow the EDA: `room_type` and `neighbourhood_group` (whose rare levels the EDA
counted), bands of the true price (quintiles plus the luxury tail above US$ 500) and the
`availability_365 == 0` flag. Every group is also measured against Ridge, the best
baseline, to show where the network's gain comes from.

Writes `code/error_numbers.json` and Figures 6-8.
"""

import json

import matplotlib

matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt  # noqa: E402
import numpy as np  # noqa: E402
import pandas as pd  # noqa: E402

from baselines import fit_baselines  # noqa: E402
from data import (  # noqa: E402
    CODE_DIR, FIG_DIR, SEED, load_data, regression_metrics, to_log, to_price,
)
from train import BASE_CONFIG, predict_price, train_model  # noqa: E402

OUT_JSON = CODE_DIR / "error_numbers.json"
BEST_CONFIG_JSON = CODE_DIR / "best_config.json"
TEST_PRED_CSV = CODE_DIR / "test_predictions.csv"
EDA_NUMBERS = CODE_DIR.parents[1] / "eda" / "code" / "eda_numbers.json"

FIG_START = 6        # Stage 5 ends at Figure 5
N_REPEATS = 5        # shuffles per column in the permutation importance
N_WORST = 10         # worst examples listed in the report
PRICE_BINS = 5       # quintiles of the true price
TAIL_PRICE = 500     # US$: the luxury tail the EDA flagged

FIG_SUBGROUP = f"fig{FIG_START:02d}-mae-by-subgroup.png"
FIG_BANDS = f"fig{FIG_START + 1:02d}-mae-by-price-band.png"
FIG_PERM = f"fig{FIG_START + 2:02d}-permutation-importance.png"

NET_COLOR = "#4C72B0"
RIDGE_COLOR = "#C44E52"


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- inputs

def resolve_mode():
    """'final' once Stage 5 has written both of its files, 'provisional' before that."""
    if BEST_CONFIG_JSON.exists() and TEST_PRED_CSV.exists():
        return "final"
    return "provisional"


def read_test_predictions(index):
    """Stage 5 predictions, reindexed to the order of `raw_test`.

    The CSV carries the row number of `data/AB_NYC_2019.csv` (0-based), which is the index
    the pipeline keeps through `clean()` and the split.
    """
    pred = pd.read_csv(TEST_PRED_CSV)
    key = "row_index" if "row_index" in pred.columns else pred.columns[0]
    pred = pred.set_index(key)
    missing = index.difference(pred.index)
    extra = pred.index.difference(index)
    if len(missing) or len(extra):
        raise SystemExit(
            f"{TEST_PRED_CSV.name} does not cover the test set: {len(missing)} test rows "
            f"missing, {len(extra)} unknown rows present. Column used as index: '{key}'."
        )
    return pred.reindex(index)


def load_eda_rho():
    """Spearman |rho| with price per numerical column, as reported in the EDA."""
    try:
        eda = json.loads(EDA_NUMBERS.read_text())
        return eda["correlation"]["spearman"]["price"]
    except (OSError, KeyError, json.JSONDecodeError):
        return {}


# ------------------------------------------------------------------- group statistics

def build_frame(raw, y_true, y_pred, y_ridge=None):
    """Original features plus the true price, the prediction and the signed error."""
    df = raw.copy()
    df["price_true"] = np.asarray(y_true, dtype=float)
    df["price_pred"] = np.asarray(y_pred, dtype=float)
    df["error"] = df["price_pred"] - df["price_true"]
    df["abs_error"] = df["error"].abs()
    if y_ridge is not None:
        df["price_ridge"] = np.asarray(y_ridge, dtype=float)
        df["abs_error_ridge"] = (df["price_ridge"] - df["price_true"]).abs()
    return df


def stats(part, total):
    """MAE in US$ and the numbers needed to read it: size, price level and bias."""
    if len(part) == 0:
        return {"n": 0, "share_pct": 0.0, "mae": None, "bias": None,
                "mean_price": None, "mae_pct_of_price": None}
    mae = float(part["abs_error"].mean())
    mean_price = float(part["price_true"].mean())
    out = {
        "n": int(len(part)),
        "share_pct": round(100 * len(part) / total, 2),
        "mae": mae,
        "bias": float(part["error"].mean()),
        "mean_price": mean_price,
        "mae_pct_of_price": round(100 * mae / mean_price, 1),
    }
    if "abs_error_ridge" in part.columns:
        mae_ridge = float(part["abs_error_ridge"].mean())
        out["mae_ridge"] = mae_ridge
        out["gain_vs_ridge_pct"] = round(100 * (mae_ridge - mae) / mae_ridge, 1)
    return out


def subgroup_rows(df, column):
    """One row per level of a categorical column, sorted by MAE (largest first)."""
    rows = [{"group": str(level), **stats(part, len(df))}
            for level, part in df.groupby(column, observed=True)]
    return sorted(rows, key=lambda r: -(r["mae"] or 0))


def price_band_rows(df):
    """Quintiles of the true price, in order, plus the luxury tail as an extra row."""
    bands = pd.qcut(df["price_true"], q=PRICE_BINS, duplicates="drop")
    rows = []
    for i, (interval, part) in enumerate(df.groupby(bands, observed=True)):
        low = df["price_true"].min() if i == 0 else interval.left
        rows.append({"band": f"US$ {low:.0f}-{interval.right:.0f}", **stats(part, len(df))})
    tail = df[df["price_true"] > TAIL_PRICE]
    rows.append({"band": f"tail: > US$ {TAIL_PRICE}", **stats(tail, len(df))})
    return rows


def availability_rows(df):
    """The 'availability_365 == 0' flag the EDA found on a third of the listings."""
    zero = df["availability_365"] == 0
    return [
        {"group": "availability_365 == 0", **stats(df[zero], len(df))},
        {"group": "availability_365 > 0", **stats(df[~zero], len(df))},
    ]


def worst_rows(df, n):
    """The n largest absolute errors, with the original features."""
    cols = ["price_true", "price_pred", "abs_error", "room_type", "neighbourhood_group",
            "neighbourhood", "minimum_nights", "number_of_reviews", "reviews_per_month",
            "calculated_host_listings_count", "availability_365", "latitude", "longitude"]
    worst = df.sort_values("abs_error", ascending=False).head(n)
    out = []
    for row_index, row in worst[cols].iterrows():
        record = {"row_index": int(row_index)}
        for col in cols:
            value = row[col]
            record[col] = value if isinstance(value, str) else float(value)
        out.append(record)
    return out


def largest_error_group(subgroups, families, min_n=0):
    """The group with the largest MAE among the given families — summary row 8."""
    best = None
    for family in families:
        for row in subgroups[family]:
            label = row.get("group") or row.get("band")
            if row["mae"] is None or row["n"] < min_n:
                continue
            if best is None or row["mae"] > best["mae"]:
                best = {"family": family, "group": label, "mae": row["mae"],
                        "n": row["n"], "mean_price": row["mean_price"]}
    return best


# ----------------------------------------------------------- permutation importance

def permutation_importance(model, pre, raw, y_true, n_repeats, seed=SEED):
    """Increase in validation MAE when one ORIGINAL column is shuffled.

    The 10 columns of the raw frame are shuffled one at a time and pushed through the
    fitted preprocessor, so one shuffle moves every one-hot column that the feature
    produces (76 of the 91 model columns come from `neighbourhood` alone).
    """
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    base_mae = float(np.mean(np.abs(
        predict_price(model, pre.transform(raw).astype(np.float32)) - y_true
    )))
    eda_rho = load_eda_rho()
    features = []
    for column in raw.columns:
        values = raw[column].to_numpy()
        deltas = []
        for _ in range(n_repeats):
            shuffled = raw.copy()
            shuffled[column] = rng.permutation(values)
            mae = float(np.mean(np.abs(
                predict_price(model, pre.transform(shuffled).astype(np.float32)) - y_true
            )))
            deltas.append(mae - base_mae)
        entry = {
            "feature": column,
            "delta_mae_mean": float(np.mean(deltas)),
            "delta_mae_std": float(np.std(deltas)),
            "deltas": [float(d) for d in deltas],
        }
        if column in eda_rho:
            entry["eda_spearman_with_price"] = eda_rho[column]
        features.append(entry)
    features.sort(key=lambda f: -f["delta_mae_mean"])
    return {"split": "validation", "base_mae": base_mae, "n_repeats": n_repeats,
            "rows": int(len(raw)), "features": features}


# ------------------------------------------------------------------------- figures

def plot_subgroups(subgroups, overall_mae, split, path):
    families = [("room_type", "Room type"), ("neighbourhood_group", "Borough")]
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4.2))
    for ax, (key, title) in zip(axes, families):
        rows = sorted(subgroups[key], key=lambda r: r["mae"])
        y = np.arange(len(rows))
        ax.barh(y, [r["mae"] for r in rows], color=NET_COLOR, label="network")
        if rows and rows[0].get("mae_ridge") is not None:
            ax.plot([r["mae_ridge"] for r in rows], y, "D", color=RIDGE_COLOR,
                    markersize=6, linestyle="none", label="Ridge")
        ax.axvline(overall_mae, color="gray", ls="--",
                   label=f"all rows (US$ {overall_mae:.2f})")
        ax.set_yticks(y, [f'{r["group"]}\n(n = {r["n"]:,})' for r in rows], fontsize=8)
        ax.set(title=title, xlabel="MAE (US$)")
        ax.legend(fontsize=8, loc="lower right")
    fig.suptitle(f"MAE by subgroup on the {split} set — network against Ridge")
    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig(FIG_DIR / path, dpi=110)
    plt.close(fig)


def plot_price_bands(rows, split, path):
    rows = [r for r in rows if r["n"] > 0]
    x = np.arange(len(rows))
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9.5, 4.6))
    ax.bar(x, [r["mae"] for r in rows], color=NET_COLOR, label="MAE of the network (US$)")
    if rows[0].get("mae_ridge") is not None:
        ax.plot(x, [r["mae_ridge"] for r in rows], "D", color=RIDGE_COLOR,
                linestyle="none", markersize=6, label="MAE of Ridge (US$)")
    ax.set_xticks(x, [f'{r["band"]}\n(n = {r["n"]:,})' for r in rows], fontsize=8)
    ax.set(xlabel="band of the true price", ylabel="MAE (US$)")
    ax2 = ax.twinx()
    ax2.plot(x, [r["mae_pct_of_price"] for r in rows], "o-", color="#55A868",
             label="MAE as % of the band's mean price")
    ax2.set_ylabel("MAE / mean price of the band (%)")
    ax2.set_ylim(0, max(r["mae_pct_of_price"] for r in rows) * 1.25)
    handles, labels = ax.get_legend_handles_labels()
    handles2, labels2 = ax2.get_legend_handles_labels()
    ax.legend(handles + handles2, labels + labels2, fontsize=8, loc="upper left")
    ax.set_title(f"MAE by band of the true price — {split} set")
    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig(FIG_DIR / path, dpi=110)
    plt.close(fig)


def plot_permutation(perm, path):
    features = perm["features"][::-1]  # ascending, so the largest ends up on top
    y = np.arange(len(features))
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.5, 4.8))
    ax.barh(y, [f["delta_mae_mean"] for f in features],
            xerr=[f["delta_mae_std"] for f in features], color=NET_COLOR, capsize=3,
            label=f"mean of {perm['n_repeats']} shuffles (± 1 std)")
    ax.axvline(0, color="gray", lw=1)
    ax.set_yticks(y, [f["feature"] for f in features], fontsize=8)
    ax.set(xlabel="increase in validation MAE when the column is shuffled (US$)",
           ylabel="original column")
    ax.set_title("Permutation importance on the validation set\n"
                 f"(unshuffled MAE US$ {perm['base_mae']:.2f}, {perm['rows']:,} rows)")
    ax.legend(fontsize=8, loc="lower right")
    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig(FIG_DIR / path, dpi=110)
    plt.close(fig)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- main

def main():
    mode = resolve_mode()
    config = dict(BASE_CONFIG)
    if mode == "final":
        config.update(json.loads(BEST_CONFIG_JSON.read_text()))
    print(f"[mode] {mode} — config: {config['hidden']}, dropout {config['dropout']}")

    d = load_data(with_test=(mode == "final"))

    # Stage 5's file is checked before anything is trained: a malformed CSV should fail in
    # a second, not after a full training run.
    pred = None
    if mode == "final":
        raw_eval, y_eval, split = d["raw_test"], d["y_test"], "test"
        pred = read_test_predictions(raw_eval.index)
        if not np.allclose(pred["price_true"].to_numpy(dtype=float), y_eval, atol=1e-6):
            raise SystemExit(
                "price_true in test_predictions.csv does not match the test target of the "
                "pipeline: Stage 5 and Stage 6 are not reading the same split."
            )
    else:
        raw_eval, y_eval, split = d["raw_val"], d["y_val"], "validation"

    model, history = train_model(d["X_train"], to_log(d["y_train"]),
                                 d["X_val"], to_log(d["y_val"]), config, seed=SEED)
    ridge = fit_baselines(d["X_train"], d["y_train"])["ridge"]

    if mode == "final":
        y_pred = pred["price_pred"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
        y_ridge = (pred["pred_ridge"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
                   if "pred_ridge" in pred.columns
                   else to_price(ridge.predict(d["X_test"])))
    else:
        y_pred = predict_price(model, d["X_val"])
        y_ridge = to_price(ridge.predict(d["X_val"]))

    df = build_frame(raw_eval, y_eval, y_pred, y_ridge)
    subgroups = {
        "room_type": subgroup_rows(df, "room_type"),
        "neighbourhood_group": subgroup_rows(df, "neighbourhood_group"),
        "price_band": price_band_rows(df),
        "availability_zero": availability_rows(df),
    }
    perm = permutation_importance(model, d["pre"], d["raw_val"], d["y_val"], N_REPEATS)

    numbers = {
        "mode": mode,
        "split": split,
        "config": {k: list(v) if isinstance(v, tuple) else v for k, v in config.items()},
        "seed": SEED,
        "model_val_mae": float(np.mean(np.abs(predict_price(model, d["X_val"])
                                              - d["y_val"]))),
        "best_epoch": history["best_epoch"],
        "rows": int(len(df)),
        "overall": regression_metrics(y_eval, y_pred),
        "overall_ridge": regression_metrics(y_eval, y_ridge),
        "subgroups": subgroups,
        "largest_error_subgroup": largest_error_group(
            subgroups, ["room_type", "neighbourhood_group", "availability_zero"]),
        "largest_error_band": largest_error_group(subgroups, ["price_band"]),
        "worst_cases": worst_rows(df, N_WORST),
        "permutation": perm,
    }
    OUT_JSON.write_text(json.dumps(numbers, indent=2))

    plot_subgroups(subgroups, numbers["overall"]["mae"], split, FIG_SUBGROUP)
    plot_price_bands(subgroups["price_band"], split, FIG_BANDS)
    plot_permutation(perm, FIG_PERM)

    print(f"[{split}] MAE US$ {numbers['overall']['mae']:.2f} "
          f"(Ridge US$ {numbers['overall_ridge']['mae']:.2f}) on {numbers['rows']:,} rows")
    print("[worst subgroup]", numbers["largest_error_subgroup"])
    print("[top 3 permutation]",
          [(f["feature"], round(f["delta_mae_mean"], 2)) for f in perm["features"][:3]])
    print(f"[files] {OUT_JSON.name}, {FIG_SUBGROUP}, {FIG_BANDS}, {FIG_PERM}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Reading Figure 6.

Entire home/apt has the largest MAE among room types (80.49) mostly because it is the most expensive group (mean US$ 210.30); in relative terms, 38.3%, it is closer to the rest.   • Staten Island is the worst subgroup on both readings: MAE US$ 108.08 and 65.6% of its mean price, with a bias of −85.85 — the largest of any group. But the number is carried by a single listing: row 22353, an Entire home/apt at US$ 5,000 predicted at US$ 153.9, contributes US$ 66.4 of the US$ 108.08 — 61% of the group's MAE. Without it Staten Island errs by US$ 42.28, in line with the Bronx. With 73 test rows, one tail listing moves the whole group.
  • Hypothesis for the pattern, not for the outlier: the two boroughs the EDA flagged as rare (Staten Island 0.77%, Bronx 2.30%) are the two with the highest relative error (65.6% and 43.9%) and the smallest gain over Ridge (2.9% and 0.8%, against 6.5% in Manhattan). Where there are few listings, the network has little local evidence and ends up close to the linear solution — it does not get the chance to earn its extra capacity.
  • Shared room repeats the pattern inside room_type: 50.9% relative error, 19 points above Private room (31.6%) at a comparable price level (US$ 74.45 against US$ 86.47). It is 2.46% of the test rows, and the EDA measured 2.34% of the dataset. Its MAE drops from 37.87 to 30.75 without its single worst listing, so part of this is the same tail effect, but the gap to Private room survives it.

The EDA flagged these 35.9% of listings as suspicious; they are 35.66% of the test set and they err less in dollars (50.81 against 57.68) and the same in relative terms (36.8% against 36.6%). With features that do not explain the tail (EDA: largest |ρ| is 0.44), the cheapest thing the optimizer can do is sit near the conditional median of the log, which in dollars is far below the tail. This is the argument that made MAE the main metric in Stage 0, now visible band by band.

Does it confirm the EDA? Partly — one prediction holds, the other does not survive the way the question is asked.

  • room_type dominates: +24.49, 4.4 times the next column, and 1.8 times the four location columns added together (+13.62). The EDA concluded that room_type is "the categorical feature that separates price the most" (Stage 3B). The network agrees, and by more than the EDA suggested.
  • Location does not come out as the most important information, which is what the EDA predicted (Stage 3A, Figure 5: "location is the most important numerical information for the price", with longitude at |ρ| = 0.44). Here longitude is fourth at +4.64, behind minimum_nights and availability_365, and latitude is eighth. Why the disagreement: the pipeline spreads location over four correlated columns, and permuting one at a time lets the other three cover for it — shuffling neighbourhood_group costs only +2.79 because the 76 neighbourhood columns still carry the borough. Dropout 0.4 makes this worse by design: it trains the network to survive missing inputs, so no single column is indispensable. The EDA's claim is about how much location explains; this table measures how much the network depends on each column alone. They are different questions, and only the second one is answered here.
  • Reviews are last, as the EDA predicted: number_of_reviews (+2.14) and reviews_per_month (+1.21) are the two smallest contributions, matching |ρ| ≤ 0.06. That they are not zero fits Section C — zero reviews is a weak marker of a listing that was never transacted, and the network does use it.
  • minimum_nights is the one ranking neither the EDA nor we expected: second, at +5.51, on a |ρ| of just 0.102. A monotonic correlation cannot see a column that matters through a nonlinear rule: a one-night minimum and a 180-night minimum describe different products at the same price point, and the network has the capacity to use that while Ridge does not.

docs.title: 7 · Conclusion
docs.text:
Was the network worth it? Stage 5 answers in one line: test MAE US$ 55.28 ± 0.08 over 5 seeds against Ridge's US$ 58.13, a gain of 4.90% where the Stage 0 criterion asked for 5%. The criterion was set before any network was trained and it was missed by US$ 0.06 of MAE. The gap to Ridge is nevertheless 34.6 times the standard deviation across seeds, so the improvement is real — it is simply smaller than what the team had decided would make the network worth adopting.

Section 6B says where those 4.9% come from, and the answer sharpens the verdict: 18.0% and 18.9% in the US$ 60–130 bands, 9.5% at the bottom, and −1.0% in the most expensive fifth, where Ridge wins. The network buys accuracy on ordinary listings, in percentage terms, and gives a little back exactly where an error costs the most dollars. Against that: 211,457 parameters instead of 92, a PyTorch dependency, a training loop with early stopping, and a hyperparameter search over 19 configurations. For a team that wants a price hint for a typical listing, the network earns its place; for anyone who cares about the expensive end of the market, Ridge is the same model with none of the cost.

Limitations.

  • The data is from 2019. It is a pre-pandemic snapshot of a market that has since changed in price level and in regulation; nothing here transfers to today without being refitted.
  • The listing text was dropped. name is the one column carrying words like "luxury", "penthouse" or "loft" — exactly the information missing to explain the tail that Sections 6B and 6C show the network cannot reach.
  • There is no outcome column. Nothing says whether a listing was ever booked, so a blocked calendar at US$ 10,000 and a real luxury apartment are identical to the model. Seven of the ten worst errors are of that kind.
  • Small subgroups are not measurable with this error distribution. Staten Island's MAE is 61% one listing; the Bronx's is 31% one listing. Any claim about a group of 73 rows, including the one in row 8 of the summary, is a claim about its worst listing.
  • The output is a point prediction with no interval, while the relative error ranges from 23.5% to 77.8% depending on the band.

Who is affected by an error. The bias is not symmetric, so the harm is not either:

  • A host with an expensive listing is told to undercharge. In the US$ 199–10,000 band the bias is −162.48 on a mean price of 361.37; a host who prices from this model gives up real revenue every booked night.
  • A host with a cheap listing is told to overcharge, by +16.68 on a mean price of 47.36 — a 35% markup that can leave the calendar empty.
  • The smallest hosts are served worst. The model is least reliable where there are fewest listings: 65.6% relative error on Staten Island, 50.9% on Shared room, and the smallest gains over Ridge in the Bronx (0.8%) and Staten Island (2.9%). A tool built on this would work better for Manhattan apartments than for the hosts with the least room to absorb a bad night.
  • A guest reading a prediction as a fair price would judge nearly every expensive listing overpriced, since 193 of the 194 listings above US$ 500 are predicted below their price.

What we would do with more time.

  1. Text features from name (TF-IDF or sentence embeddings) — the cheapest likely gain, given that the tail is the main source of error.
  2. An "is it active" proxy from reviews and availability, to flag or drop the placeholder listings that dominate the worst cases instead of training against them.
  3. Quantile regression, or a two-stage model that first classifies "tail", to report an interval instead of optimizing a single point for a distribution this skewed.
  4. Target encoding for neighbourhood instead of 76 one-hot columns, which would also make the importance of location readable in a single number rather than split across four columns.

docs.title: Como usar este template
docs.text: Este repositório gera o site de entregas da disciplina. O fluxo é sempre o mesmo: você edita um Markdown (ou commita um notebook) dentro de docs/, dá git push na main, e o GitHub Actions publica o site.

docs.title: Estrutura de pastas
docs.text:
Os nomes abaixo são um contrato com a correção — não os renomeie.

estrutura
docs/
  index.md                       # capa: grupo e status das entregas
  exercises/
    data/
      index.md                   # o relatório
      code/                      # scripts, como arquivos executáveis
      figures/                   # imagens commitadas
    perceptron/
    mlp/
    vae/
  projects/
    index.md                     # visão geral: equipe, dataset, as 3 entregas
    eda/
      index.md
      code/
      figures/
    classification/              # escolha classification OU regression
    regression/                  # e apague a pasta que sobrar
    generative/
mkdocs.yml
requirements.txt

Cada entrega tem a própria pasta, sempre com o mesmo formato: index.md para o relatório, code/ para os scripts e figures/ para as imagens. Se a entrega for um notebook, ele entra na mesma pasta — data/index.ipynb no lugar de data/index.md.

O projeto é um só: as três entregas de projects/ compartilham equipe e dataset, e a segunda é classificação ou regressão, nunca as duas.

O conjunto de entregas muda de edição para edição

Os slugs acima são os das edições recentes. Confira a lista da sua edição no overview da disciplina e ajuste duas coisas em conjunto: as pastas em docs/ e a nav do mkdocs.yml. Cada nova entrega é uma pasta com index.md, code/ e figures/ — copie uma existente.

docs.title: Front matter obrigatório
docs.text:
Todo relatório começa com:

docs/exercises/<slug>/index.md
---
exercise: data
ai_use: "descreva o uso de IA, ou 'none'"
---

Nos projetos, troque exercise: por project: (eda, classification, regression, generative). Os dois campos são obrigatórios.

docs.title: Colocando uma entrega no menu
docs.text: Um item de menu por entrega, em mkdocs.yml. O alvo pode ser Markdown, notebook .ipynb ou um link do Colab — os três exemplos estão em Exemplos de uso.

docs.title: Antes de publicar
docs.text:
Todas as linhas do mkdocs.yml que você precisa trocar estão marcadas com # TROCAR:

mkdocs.yml
site_name: ANN-DL · Entregas                  # TROCAR: título exibido no topo do site
site_author: Seu Nome, Sobrenome              # TROCAR: seu nome (ou os nomes do grupo)
site_url: https://usuario.github.io/ann-dl    # TROCAR: https://<seu-usuario>.github.io/<seu-repo>
repo_url: https://github.com/usuario/ann-dl   # TROCAR: https://github.com/<seu-usuario>/<seu-repo>
repo_name: usuario/ann-dl                     # TROCAR: <seu-usuario>/<seu-repo>

Há mais uma no nav, na URL do Colab. Para achar todas:

grep -n "TROCAR" mkdocs.yml

O passo a passo completo está em Publicação no GitHub Pages.

docs.title: Pré-requisitos
docs.text:
Antes de começar, certifique-se de que você possui os seguintes pré-requisitos instalados em seu sistema:

  • Git: Para clonar o repositório.

docs.title: Instalando o Python
docs.text:
Python 3.10 ou superior. O GitHub Actions constrói o site com a versão definida em PYTHON_VERSION, no workflow — usar localmente a mesma versão evita surpresas entre o seu build e o do CI.

LinuxmacOSWindows

Instale o Python 3.10 ou superior.

sudo apt install python3 python3-venv python3-pip
python3 --version

Instale o Python 3.10 ou superior.

brew install python
python3 --version

Instale o Python 3.10 ou superior. Baixe o instalador do site oficial do Python (https://www.python.org/downloads/) e execute-o. Certifique-se de marcar a opção "Add Python to PATH" durante a instalação.

python --version

docs.title: Instalando as dependências
docs.text:
Para rodar o site na sua máquina, siga os passos a seguir.

Clone ou fork este repositório:

git clone <URL_DO_REPOSITORIO>

Crie um ambiente virtual do Python:

Linux/macOSWindows 
python3 -m venv env

python -m venv env

Ative o ambiente virtual (você deve fazer isso sempre que for executar algum script deste repositório):

Linux/macOSWindows 
source ./env/bin/activate

.\env\Scripts\activate

Instale as dependências com:

Linux/macOSWindows 
python3 -m pip install -r requirements.txt --upgrade

python -m pip install -r requirements.txt --upgrade

docs.title: Publicação no GitHub Pages
docs.text:
O site não é publicado a partir da main: o GitHub Actions constrói o HTML e o empurra para uma branch separada, gh-pages, e é ela que o GitHub Pages serve.

flowchart LR
    push["git push<br/>branch main"] --> ci["GitHub Actions<br/>mkdocs gh-deploy --force"]
    ci -->|escreve| gp["branch gh-pages<br/>(HTML gerado)"]
    gp --> pages["GitHub Pages<br/>usuario.github.io/repo"]

Isso significa que você nunca edita a gh-pages à mão — ela é reescrita a cada push.

Os passos 1 a 4 são feitos uma única vez. Depois disso, publicar é dar git push.

docs.title: Passo 1 — Repositório público e Actions habilitado
docs.text:
Registre o repositório no formulário da disciplina uma vez, no começo do semestre, e o mantenha público: a correção lê o site e o repositório, e o GitHub Pages exige repositório público em contas gratuitas.

Se você usou Fork, os workflows vêm desligados

Em um fork, o GitHub desabilita o Actions por segurança. Abra a aba Actions do seu repositório e clique em I understand my workflows, go ahead and enable them. Sem isso, o push não dispara build nenhum e o site nunca aparece.

Usando Use this template em vez de Fork, o Actions já vem ligado — e o histórico começa limpo, o que é preferível, já que o prazo é medido pelos seus commits.

docs.title: Passo 2 — Garantir que o CI possa escrever
docs.text:
O workflow precisa escrever na branch gh-pages, e o token do Actions não tem esse escopo por padrão. O workflow deste template já o pede explicitamente:

.github/workflows/main.yaml
permissions:
  contents: write

Esse bloco sobrepõe o padrão do repositório, então normalmente não há nada a fazer aqui. Ele só não basta em dois casos: se você removeu o bloco, ou se uma política do repositório ou da organização impede que o workflow eleve o próprio escopo.

Se o build falhar no último passo

O sintoma é remote: Permission to <usuario>/<repo>.git denied to github-actions[bot] ou error: failed to push some refs. A correção é em Settings → Actions → General → Workflow permissions: marque Read and write permissions, salve, e re-execute o workflow em Actions → (o run que falhou) → Re-run all jobs.

Settings → Actions → General → Workflow permissions

O workflow completo:

.github/workflows/main.yaml
name: ci
on:
  push:
  pull_request:
  # Permite disparar o build à mão em Actions > ci > Run workflow, sem precisar
  # de um commit novo.
  workflow_dispatch:

# Environment
env:
  CI: true
  PYTHON_VERSION: 3.12

# O job precisa escrever na branch gh-pages.
# Isto só tem efeito se, em Settings > Actions > General > Workflow permissions,
# a opção "Read and write permissions" estiver marcada.
permissions:
  contents: write

# Jobs to run
jobs:

  # Build and deploy documentation site
  deploy:
    if: github.event_name != 'pull_request' && github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:

      # Checkout source from GitHub.
      # fetch-depth: 0 traz o histórico completo — sem ele os plugins git-authors e
      # git-revision-date-localized não conseguem datar as páginas.
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0

      # Install Python runtime and dependencies
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: ${{ env.PYTHON_VERSION }}

      # pip
      - run: |
          pip install -r requirements.txt

      # deploy
      - run: |
          mkdocs gh-deploy --force

docs.title: Passo 3 — Publicar
docs.text:
git add .
git commit -m "exercises/data: relatório do exercício 1"
git push

Acompanhe em Actions. O primeiro run cria a branch gh-pages; leva 1–2 minutos.

Disparar sem commit

O workflow também aceita disparo manual: Actions → ci → Run workflow. Útil para republicar depois de mexer numa configuração do GitHub, sem precisar inventar um commit.

O prazo é o seu último commit

O prazo de uma entrega é o timestamp do último commit que toca a pasta daquela entrega — não a hora do formulário nem a da publicação. Commite ao longo do trabalho, não tudo no minuto do prazo.

docs.title: Passo 4 — Apontar o Pages para a branch gh-pages
docs.text:
Só depois que o primeiro run terminar (a branch precisa existir): em Settings → Pages, em Build and deployment, escolha Deploy from a branch, selecione a branch gh-pages e a pasta / (root), e salve.

Settings → Pages → Build and deployment

O endereço aparece no topo dessa mesma tela, no formato https://<seu-usuario>.github.io/<seu-repo>/. Ele precisa ser idêntico ao site_url do mkdocs.yml — é dele que o Material monta os links do menu e o sitemap.xml.

docs.title: Passo 5 — Conferir
docs.text:
• O run em Actions terminou com o check verde.
  • A branch gh-pages existe e tem um index.html na raiz.
  • A URL de Settings → Pages abre o site.
  • O menu tem as suas entregas, e nenhum link quebrado.
  • Nada de usuario/ann-dl sobrou: grep -rn "TROCAR\|usuario/ann-dl" mkdocs.yml docs/

docs.title: Validando antes do push
docs.text:
O CI publica mesmo com avisos; o modo estrito, não. Rode localmente antes de commitar:

mkdocs serve -o                  # preview com recarga automática
mkdocs build --strict            # falha em link quebrado ou snippet inexistente

docs.title: Publicação manual
docs.text:
Se precisar publicar sem esperar o CI — ou se o Actions estiver indisponível:

mkdocs gh-deploy

O comando constrói o site e empurra para a gh-pages usando as suas credenciais do Git. Ele não substitui o Passo 2: assim que você voltar a dar push na main, quem publica é o CI.

docs.title: Quando não funcionar
docs.text: Sintoma Causa provável Nenhum run aparece em Actions depois de um push Workflows desabilitados no fork (Passo 1) — o botão Run workflow pode funcionar mesmo assim Run falha com Permission ... denied to github-actions[bot] O permissions: do workflow foi removido, ou a política do repositório bloqueia a elevação (Passo 2) Settings → Pages não oferece a branch gh-pages O primeiro run ainda não terminou (Passo 3) Site abre em 404 Fonte do Pages não configurada (Passo 4), ou repositório privado Site abre, mas CSS e links estão quebrados site_url diferente da URL real do Pages Build falha em Snippet at path ... could not be found --8<-- apontando para arquivo que não existe ou não foi commitado Notebook aparece sem os gráficos O .ipynb foi commitado sem as saídas salvas — o CI roda com execute: false
